drug_class: PARP inhibitor (a type of targeted cancer therapy)
purpose: Niraparib is used to treat certain types of ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, and primary peritoneal cancer. It is often given to help keep cancer from coming back after chemotherapy has worked. It may also be used as a first treatment for advanced ovarian cancer in some patients.
how_it_works: Cancer cells sometimes have broken DNA repair systems that they rely on to survive and grow. Niraparib blocks a protein called PARP, which cancer cells need to fix their damaged DNA. By blocking PARP, the drug causes cancer cells to build up so much DNA damage that they die, while healthy cells are better able to cope.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, constipation, or stomach pain are very common, especially early on. You may also feel very tired, have headaches, or notice a decreased appetite. Blood count changes are common — your red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets may drop, which is why you will need regular blood tests. Some people experience high blood pressure or trouble sleeping.
warnings: This medication can cause serious drops in blood counts, which can increase your risk of infection, bleeding, or anemia — tell your doctor right away if you have a fever, unusual bruising, or feel unusually short of breath. Rarely, it can cause a serious blood or bone marrow problem called MDS or AML. Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm a baby. Always tell your doctor about all other medications you take, including supplements.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 200 mg or 300 mg taken by mouth once a day, depending on your body weight and platelet levels. It comes as a capsule and is typically taken at the same time each day, with or without food. Taking it at bedtime may help reduce nausea. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how your body responds and your blood test results.
